chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn Hilal, from Muhammad ibn Sinan who said:

I said to Abu Al-Hasan Al-Rida (peace be upon him), during the days of Harun, 'You have made yourself known by this Command, and you are sitting in the seat of your father, while the sword of Harun drips with blood.' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'What encouraged me to do this is what the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: If Abu Jahl takes a single hair from my head, then testify that I am not a Prophet, and I say to you: If Harun takes a single hair from my head, then testify that I am not an Imam.'

key_terms.أَبُو جَهْلٍ: Abu Jahl (Jahl ibn Hisham, a chief opponent of the Prophet)
key_terms.هَارُونُ: Harun (referring to Harun al-Rashid, the Abbasid Caliph)

ai.seo_question: How did Imam Al-Rida justify his public declaration of Imamate during the time of Harun al-Rashid?
ai.summary: Imam Al-Rida (peace be upon him) justifies his public declaration of Imamate during the reign of Harun al-Rashid by drawing a direct parallel to the Prophet Muhammad’s challenge to Abu Jahl, asserting that his authority is divinely grounded rather than dependent on political validation. This analogy underscores the continuity of divine proof (Hujjah), where the Imam’s status is as undeniable as the Prophet’s, even amidst the threat of the Caliph’s sword. The reference to Abu Jahl highlights the theme of confronting powerful disbelievers who deny divine appointment, reinforcing the Imam’s confidence in his God-given mandate.
